one_liner: Open-source MASM-syntax x86/x64 assembler descended from JWasm; forum timings put it modestly ahead of MASM, behind JWasm and AsmC.
what_it_does: UASM is a command-line assembler that accepts Microsoft MASM syntax (ml/ml64 style sources, macros, INVOKE, structs, records) for 16-, 32- and 64-bit x86 and writes OMF, COFF, Win64, ELF32/64, Mach-O 64, MZ, PE or flat binary output, so the same MASM-style source can be built on Windows, Linux, macOS and DOS. Beyond MASM it adds instruction coverage up to AVX-512 and MPX, SystemV, VECTORCALL and Borland calling conventions for INVOKE, C-style string literals, and a built-in macro library (OO helpers, 128-bit moves and shifts, MEMALLOC). It is close to a drop-in for ml/ml64 on most sources, with documented and reported differences.
how_it_is_fast: The speed comes from JWasm's design, which UASM keeps. 'Fastpass' (fastpass.c) stores preprocessed lines in memory during pass 1 and replays them in later passes instead of re-reading and re-expanding the source and include files; '-nfp' turns it off. FASTMEM (memalloc.c) is a bump allocator over 512 KB chunks taken from VirtualAlloc or mmap. A larger symbol hash table (2003 to 8009 buckets) gave JWasm a 10-20% speed-up on symbol-heavy sources (History.txt). Nothing in the repo measures UASM's own speed.
when_to_use: Building existing MASM-syntax code (masm32-style projects, hand-written x64 kernels) on Linux or macOS, or anywhere ml64 is unavailable or unlicensed
Sources that need AVX-512 or other recent instructions together with MASM macros, INVOKE and calling-convention helpers for both Win64 and SystemV
Large single-file sources where JWasm-style fastpass beats MASM's re-reading passes (forum anecdote: 21,000 lines in 1630 ms vs 1800 ms for MASM 6.15/10.0)
Projects that already rely on UASM extensions (OO macro library, string literals, @Platform/@Arch built-ins) that ml64 does not have
when_not_to_use: When raw assembly speed is the goal: in the same forum tests AsmC (1200 ms) and JWasm (1480 ms) beat UASM's 1630 ms, and on the m32lib build UAsm64 took 7285 ticks vs JWasm 4867 and AsmC 4181
Toolchains on GCC 15 or recent clang without extra flags: open build failures #228/#233 (C23 'bool' typedef in H/bool.h), #232, #211 (-fwritable-strings), #197 (clang), #183/#148 (macOS)

Code that needs bit-exact MASM behaviour: open reports of MASM-inconsistent RECORD operations (#230), wrong encodings (#213 vpextrw, #225 SHRX family, fixed only on the unreleased v2.58 branch), ignored unnamed Unicode string data (#221) and missing CodeView line data (#234)
Shipping modified builds inside a company without publishing them: the Open Watcom licence counts internal business use as 'Deploy' and then requires the modified source to be published
New code targeting Intel APX or other post-AVX-512 extensions (#209 open)

integration.form: command-line executable built from C source (no GitHub releases; binaries are offered on terraspace.co.uk, not checked here)
integration.dependencies: none beyond a C compiler and the C runtime
integration.min_toolchain: near-C89 C with 64-bit integers; makefiles for GCC, clang, MSVC (VS2019 solution), Open Watcom, Intel C, Pelles C and others. GCC 10+/clang 11+ need -fcommon; GCC 15's C23 default fails on 'typedef unsigned char bool' (#228); forcing an older -std probably works but is not documented
integration.platforms: hosts: Windows, Linux, macOS, DOS; targets: x86 16/32/64-bit code only
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded tool built on global assembler state (ModuleInfo, the fastpass LineStore); the DLL build (MsvcDll.mak) is not reentrant
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: accepts most MASM/ml64 syntax and command-line conventions, but encodings and edge-case semantics differ on open issues, and UASM extensions are not accepted by MASM

gotchas: master is stale: it stops at version 2.53pre (last commit 2022-03-16, the date the catalogue records), but development continues on per-version branches: v2.57 (2024-08-12) and v2.58, still marked 'pre' in H/globals.h, last committed 2025-11-30. Build from the latest vNN branch, not master.

The built-in macro library is expanded on pass 1 of every module unless you pass -nomlib. This is a fixed per-file cost and may be one reason UASM trails JWasm on many-small-file builds such as m32lib (untested). Its 64-bit SHIFTLEFT128 macro ends with 'mov rcx,savercx' then 'mov rcx,saversi', so it returns with rcx holding the caller's rsi and rsi still pointing at the operand (macrolib.c, v2.58). The 128-bit shift macros also save registers in static .data? slots, which makes the generated code non-reentrant.

No benchmark harness exists: every speed number is a masm32.com forum anecdote (jj2007, 2020) seen only in search snippets, with no hardware or exact versions. Other snippets disagree on the MASM margin: newer ML64 'only about 40% slower' versus ML '3-5x slower' than UASM, and for UASM's predecessor HJWasm, 12551 ms vs ML 10.0 16356 ms on m32lib.
Readme.txt and Doc/ are still JWasm's original texts, and History.txt stops at 2.40, so the changes in 2.41-2.58 are documented only in commits and on the unreachable project site.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among MASM-compatible assemblers, AsmC and JWasm are faster on every forum timing; pick UASM only when you need its extensions (AVX-512 and MPX coverage, SystemV/VECTORCALL INVOKE, Mach-O output, the OO macro library) or already have UASM-dialect sources. Disassemblers such as iced or Zydis solve a different problem.
verified_claims_summary: One masm32.com forum user (jj2007, April 2020; snippet only, no hardware or flags) assembled a 21,000-line MASM source in 1630 ms with UAsm64 against 1800 ms with MASM 6.15 and 10.0 (about 1.1x), while JWasm took 1480 ms and AsmC 1200 ms. Other thread snippets give UASM a 1.4x to 5x lead over various ML versions but put it about 25% behind AsmC. Nothing is reproducible.
status_note: Not abandoned as recorded: master froze at 2.53pre in March 2022, but the v2.58 branch had fixes through 2025-11-30 (SHRX encoding, NOT operator, RECORD, djgpp). Activity is slow, many build and encoding issues stay open without maintainer replies, there are no GitHub releases, and the Sybase Open Watcom Public License 1.0 (License.txt) requires publishing source of modified builds that are deployed, including internal business use.
